An audience is not a business

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 6 July 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

In short: An audience is an asset, not a business. A media business starts when you can say who the audience is, what it does, who pays for access to it, and which part of it you actually own. The market has made that test harder to dodge. The Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found that social and video platforms are now the most used route to online news, ahead of publishers' own sites and apps, and only 17% of people in 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news in the past year.

Key points

  • A media company sells to at least three buyers, readers, sponsors and licensees, plus an investor. Each buys something different.
  • Reach is the weakest claim. Composition and behaviour, what the audience decides, buys or builds, is the claim buyers pay for.
  • Report the owned audience first and separately. Rented platform reach exists to feed the owned list.
  • The editorial point of view is the product truth. If nobody could disagree with it, it is a category description.
  • Tag every external audience number as verified, platform-reported or estimated. Buying fake follower counts is now a US federal rule violation.

Three buyers and an investor

Most media founders pitch one thing to everyone: size. That fails because a media company sells to at least three different buyers.

Readers and subscribers buy time saved, judgement they trust, or access they cannot get elsewhere. The Reuters Institute found the most common reason people give for paying for news is "to get useful content I can't access any other way", with 81% citing a direct benefit of some kind. Advertisers and sponsors buy attention from a specific kind of person at a specific moment. Licensees and data buyers buy content or signals they can use inside their own products. Then there is the investor, who buys the future cash flows of all of the above.

Our piece on one truth and three audiences covers one product truth and a belief per audience. In media that discipline matters more, because the buyers are so unlike each other. The reader does not care about your CPM. The sponsor does not care about your editorial mission unless it explains who reads you.

BuyerWhat they buyThe belief that must be trueProof they accept
Reader or subscriberTime saved, trusted judgement, access"I get something here I cannot get free elsewhere"Sampling, renewal, word of mouth
Sponsor or advertiserAttention from a defined person at a defined moment"These are the people I sell to, and they respond"Verified composition, past response
Licensee or data buyerContent or signals for their own product"This is original, usable and legally clean"Rights, format, update frequency
InvestorFuture cash flows of all three"This revenue repeats and does not depend on one platform"Owned audience, retention, revenue mix

Write the four beliefs down. If two of them are the same sentence, you have not done the work.

Reach is the weakest claim

Reach is easy to state and easy to discount. Everyone has a number, most of them are platform-reported, and buyers have learned to divide them by something.

Buyers have reason to be sceptical. The IAB's 2025 creator economy study, a trade body survey of US ad buyers, listed standards for audience authentication and fraud prevention among the main gaps buyers want closed. In August 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission finalised a rule that bans buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as bot-generated followers or views, where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them to misrepresent influence for a commercial purpose. An inflated follower count is no longer only a credibility problem.

The stronger claim is about composition and behaviour. Who are these people, and what do they do? Three verbs matter most to the people who pay you:

VerbWhat it means for the audienceWho pays for it
DecidesSigns off budgets, policy, hiring, vendorsSponsors, B2B data buyers
BuysPurchases in a category you coverAffiliates, commerce partners, sponsors
BuildsShips products or code in your fieldTooling sponsors, recruiters, licensees

A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls. Your positioning should state the verb, the category, and the proof.

"Read by people who run treasury at mid-sized funds" is a position. "Two hundred thousand followers" is a number.

A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls.

Owned versus rented

Every media business has two audiences and only one of them is yours.

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill, the subscribers whose details sit in your systems. You set the rules, you can move platforms, and nobody can throttle you.

The rented audience is everyone who follows you on a platform. The platform owns the relationship, the algorithm, the data, and the right to change the terms tomorrow. That last right is exercised often. X closed new enrolments to its Creator Revenue Sharing programme on 7 August 2026 and ended its earnings on 7 September 2026, moving creators to a new Original Content Rewards programme with its own eligibility tests.

The rented side is growing. The Reuters Institute found 54% of people now use social and video networks to get news online, against 51% for news websites and apps, and that publishers' own sites and apps have lost 12 percentage points of reach since 2021. Its 2026 trends survey of 280 media leaders found 70% concerned about competition from creators and influencers.

Rented reach has a job: it feeds the owned list. That is its whole purpose in a commercial model. If your rented numbers are growing and your owned numbers are flat, you are building someone else's asset.

State the owned number first, clearly and separately, and treat the rest as a funnel. Our build order for media and publishing applies the same logic to which revenue decisions a publisher should record first.

Editorial point of view is the product truth

In most verticals the product truth is a feature or an outcome. In media it is the point of view.

A point of view is what makes someone read you instead of the free summary. It is why a sponsor wants to appear next to you and not next to a competitor with the same audience size. It is why a licensee pays for your version of a story that exists elsewhere.

The free summary is now a real competitor. Weekly use of AI chatbots for news rose from 7% to 10% in a year, according to the Reuters Institute, and 16% among under-35s. A publication with no distinct view is easy for a summary to replace.

Write it in one sentence. It should be something a reasonable person in your field could disagree with. If nobody could disagree, it is not a point of view, it is a category description.

Everything downstream, from the subscription pitch to the sponsor deck, should be able to trace back to that sentence.

A claims register for audience numbers

Our piece on one truth and three audiences introduced the claims register. Media needs its own version because audience figures are the claims buyers check hardest.

Keep one sheet with every number you use externally. For each, record the source and the status:

StatusExamplesWhere it can appear
VerifiedEmail list size, paid subscribers, renewal counts; from your own systems, exportable, auditableInvestor and sponsor materials without a label
Platform-reportedFollowers, impressions, listens; from a dashboard you do not controlAnywhere, with a label every time
EstimatedHousehold reach, pass-along, total audience; derived or modelledOut of the deck unless you can show the method

The register also protects the founder. Goldman Sachs Research estimated in 2023 that about 4% of the world's roughly 50 million creators earn more than $100,000 a year, and that brand deals make up about 70% of creator revenue. When most income comes from selling access to an audience, buyers check the numbers. A register answers before they ask. The same discipline runs through our piece on commercial KPIs a board will trust.

This register is usually the first document we build with a media client, because it tends to change the pitch before anyone writes a slide.

lowob takeaways

  • Write four beliefs. One each for the reader, the sponsor, the licensee and the investor, and no two the same.
  • Position on behaviour. State what the audience decides, buys or builds, not how many there are.
  • Owned first, rented second. Report the owned audience separately; give rented reach the job of feeding it.
  • Register every number. Verified, platform-reported or estimated, with estimates kept out of the deck without a method.
Gateway card

Before the next sponsor or investor deck

  • One belief written for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee, investor
  • Positioning that states what the audience does, not how many there are
  • Owned audience reported separately from rented audience, owned first
  • Editorial point of view in one sentence someone could disagree with
  • Claims register with every external number tagged verified, platform-reported or estimated
  • Each rented channel given an explicit job: feeding the owned list

Common questions

How should a media startup pitch its audience to investors and sponsors?

Write a separate belief for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee and investor. Position on what the audience does, such as deciding, buying or building, and lead with the owned audience you can export.

What is the difference between an owned and a rented audience?

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill and the subscribers in your own systems. The rented audience is your platform followers, where the platform owns the relationship, the algorithm, the data and the terms.

Which audience numbers can go in an investor deck?

Only verified numbers from your own systems go in without a label. Platform-reported numbers get a label every time, and estimates stay out unless you can show the method.

Is it illegal to buy followers for a media business?

In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule bans buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence when the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them to misrepresent influence commercially.

Sources and notes

  • Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary, June 2026. Large online survey across 48 markets; payment figures cover 20 markets where paywalls are common.
  • Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026, 12 January 2026. Survey of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries; a strategic sample, not representative.
  • Federal Trade Commission, Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials, 14 August 2024. US regulator; applies to US commerce.
  • IAB, Creator economy ad spend to reach $37 billion in 2025, 20 November 2025. Trade body study of US ad buyers; sample size not stated in the release.
  • Goldman Sachs, The creator economy could approach half-a-trillion dollars by 2027, 19 April 2023. Investment bank research; a market sizing projection, and older than the other sources.
  • X Help Center, Original Content Rewards Program, accessed November 2026. Platform documentation; terms change without notice.
  • The buyer table and the claims register are lowob's framework.
